Inferencia estadística en R: confianza y significación

Contrastes sobre media y varianza (una y dos poblaciones) + normalidad y aleatoriedad.
R
Estadística
Inferencia
Author

Hugo Sánchez Nieto

Published

January 1, 2026

Objetivo

Realizar inferencia sobre media y varianza en una y dos poblaciones, usando t.test() y var.test(), y cerrar con comprobaciones típicas: normalidad y aleatoriedad.

Preparación

Usaremos el dataset cars (incluido en R).

data(cars)
speed <- cars$speed
dist  <- cars$dist
library(nortest)  # lillie.test
library(tseries)  # runs.test
library(car)      # leveneTest

1) p-valor y decisión

El p-valor se usa para decidir si rechazamos H0 al nivel de significación elegido (10%, 5%, 1%).

Creo un helper para imprimir decisiones de forma uniforme:

decision <- function(p, alpha = 0.05, h0 = "H0") {
  if (is.na(p)) return("p-value NA")
  if (p < alpha) paste("Rechazo", h0, "(p <", alpha, ")")
  else paste("No rechazo", h0, "(p ≥", alpha, ")")
}

2) Inferencia para una población (media)

Ejemplo clásico: contrastar si la media de speed es 17, con contrastes bilateral y unilaterales (greater/less).

t_2colas <- t.test(speed, mu = 17)  # por defecto: two.sided
t_mayor  <- t.test(speed, mu = 17, alternative = "greater")
t_menor  <- t.test(speed, mu = 17, alternative = "less")

t_2colas

    One Sample t-test

data:  speed
t = -2.1397, df = 49, p-value = 0.03739
alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 17
95 percent confidence interval:
 13.89727 16.90273
sample estimates:
mean of x 
     15.4 
cat(decision(t_2colas$p.value, h0 = "media = 17"), "\n\n")
Rechazo media = 17 (p < 0.05 ) 
t_mayor

    One Sample t-test

data:  speed
t = -2.1397, df = 49, p-value = 0.9813
alternative hypothesis: true mean is greater than 17
95 percent confidence interval:
 14.1463     Inf
sample estimates:
mean of x 
     15.4 
cat(decision(t_mayor$p.value, h0 = "media = 17 (alt: mayor)"), "\n\n")
No rechazo media = 17 (alt: mayor) (p ≥ 0.05 ) 
t_menor

    One Sample t-test

data:  speed
t = -2.1397, df = 49, p-value = 0.01869
alternative hypothesis: true mean is less than 17
95 percent confidence interval:
    -Inf 16.6537
sample estimates:
mean of x 
     15.4 
cat(decision(t_menor$p.value, h0 = "media = 17 (alt: menor)"), "\n")
Rechazo media = 17 (alt: menor) (p < 0.05 )

Región de rechazo

En el temario también compara el valor experimental con el teórico (qt)

qt(0.975, df = length(speed) - 1)  # dos colas al 5%
[1] 2.009575
qt(0.95,  df = length(speed) - 1)  # una cola (greater) al 5%
[1] 1.676551
qt(0.05,  df = length(speed) - 1)  # una cola (less) al 5%
[1] -1.676551

3) Inferencia para dos poblaciones (varianzas y medias)

3.1 Igualdad de varianzas (F-test)

Comparamos speed y dist con var.test(), tanto bilateral como unilateral (por ejemplo, ratio < 1)

var(speed); var(dist)
[1] 27.95918
[1] 664.0608
f_2colas <- var.test(speed, dist)
f_menor  <- var.test(speed, dist, alternative = "less")

f_2colas

    F test to compare two variances

data:  speed and dist
F = 0.042103, num df = 49, denom df = 49, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true ratio of variances is not equal to 1
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.02389265 0.07419404
sample estimates:
ratio of variances 
        0.04210335 
cat(decision(f_2colas$p.value, h0 = "varianzas iguales (two.sided)"), "\n\n")
Rechazo varianzas iguales (two.sided) (p < 0.05 ) 
f_menor

    F test to compare two variances

data:  speed and dist
F = 0.042103, num df = 49, denom df = 49, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true ratio of variances is less than 1
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.00000000 0.06767227
sample estimates:
ratio of variances 
        0.04210335 
cat(decision(f_menor$p.value, h0 = "ratio de varianzas = 1 (alt: < 1)"), "\n")
Rechazo ratio de varianzas = 1 (alt: < 1) (p < 0.05 )

Región crítica

qf(0.025, df1 = length(speed)-1, df2 = length(dist)-1)
[1] 0.5674762
qf(0.975, df1 = length(speed)-1, df2 = length(dist)-1)
[1] 1.762189

3.2 Igualdad de medias (t-test para dos muestras)

Si no asumimos varianzas iguales, usamos Welch (var.equal = FALSE, que es el valor por defecto)

t2_2colas <- t.test(speed, dist, var.equal = FALSE)
t2_2colas

    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  speed and dist
t = -7.4134, df = 53.119, p-value = 9.628e-10
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -35.04152 -20.11848
sample estimates:
mean of x mean of y 
    15.40     42.98 
cat(decision(t2_2colas$p.value, h0 = "medias iguales (Welch)"), "\n")
Rechazo medias iguales (Welch) (p < 0.05 )

Unilateral (por ejemplo, media de speed menor que dist):

t2_menor <- t.test(speed, dist, var.equal = FALSE, alternative = "less")
t2_menor

    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  speed and dist
t = -7.4134, df = 53.119, p-value = 4.814e-10
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is less than 0
95 percent confidence interval:
      -Inf -21.35209
sample estimates:
mean of x mean of y 
    15.40     42.98 
cat(decision(t2_menor$p.value, h0 = "medias iguales (alt: speed < dist)"), "\n")
Rechazo medias iguales (alt: speed < dist) (p < 0.05 )

Región crítica

qt(0.975, df = t2_2colas$parameter)  # df de Welch
[1] 2.005641

4) Inferencia con más de dos grupos (ANOVA) + homogeneidad de varianzas

El temario construye un factor con 3 niveles (0,1,2) y hace:

  • resúmenes por grupo (tapply)

  • ANOVA (aov)

  • Levene (homogeneidad de varianzas)

  • TukeyHSD (comparaciones por pares)

set.seed(2022)
terna <- rbinom(length(speed), 2, 0.5)
factores_terna <- factor(terna)

table(factores_terna)
factores_terna
 0  1  2 
13 23 14 
tapply(speed, factores_terna, summary)
$`0`
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   7.00   10.00   12.00   13.38   15.00   24.00 

$`1`
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
    4.0    12.5    17.0    15.7    19.5    24.0 

$`2`
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   4.00   14.00   16.50   16.79   20.00   25.00 
tapply(speed, factores_terna, var)
       0        1        2 
22.75641 27.31225 31.87363 
anova_speed <- aov(speed ~ factores_terna)

leveneTest(speed ~ factores_terna, center = mean)
Levene's Test for Homogeneity of Variance (center = mean)
      Df F value Pr(>F)
group  2  0.1895  0.828
      47               
summary(anova_speed)
               Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)
factores_terna  2   81.7   40.85    1.49  0.236
Residuals      47 1288.3   27.41               
TukeyHSD(anova_speed)
  Tukey multiple comparisons of means
    95% family-wise confidence level

Fit: aov(formula = speed ~ factores_terna)

$factores_terna
        diff       lwr      upr     p adj
1-0 2.311037 -2.085524 6.707597 0.4177758
2-0 3.401099 -1.479168 8.281366 0.2209356
2-1 1.090062 -3.205008 5.385133 0.8130943

No rechazo homogeneidad de varianzas (Levene, p=0.828). No rechazo igualdad de medias (ANOVA, p=0.236).

5) Hipótesis de partida: normalidad y aleatoriedad

5.1 Normalidad

En el temario se aplican KS, Shapiro y Lilliefors, y se recuerda que si p-valor > 0.05 no se rechaza normalidad.

ks <- ks.test(speed, pnorm, mean(speed), sd(speed))
Warning in ks.test.default(speed, pnorm, mean(speed), sd(speed)): ties should
not be present for the one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test
sw <- shapiro.test(speed)
lf <- lillie.test(speed)

ks; cat(decision(ks$p.value, h0="normalidad (KS)"), "\n\n")

    Asymptotic one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test

data:  speed
D = 0.068539, p-value = 0.9729
alternative hypothesis: two-sided
No rechazo normalidad (KS) (p ≥ 0.05 ) 
sw; cat(decision(sw$p.value, h0="normalidad (Shapiro)"), "\n\n")

    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  speed
W = 0.97765, p-value = 0.4576
No rechazo normalidad (Shapiro) (p ≥ 0.05 ) 
lf; cat(decision(lf$p.value, h0="normalidad (Lilliefors)"), "\n")

    Lilliefors (Kolmogorov-Smirnov) normality test

data:  speed
D = 0.068539, p-value = 0.8068
No rechazo normalidad (Lilliefors) (p ≥ 0.05 )

5.2 Aleatoriedad (test de rachas)

Se contrasta H0: “hay aleatoriedad” usando runs.test() sobre la variable binaria speed > median(speed)

runs <- runs.test(as.factor(speed > median(speed)))
runs

    Runs Test

data:  as.factor(speed > median(speed))
Standard Normal = -6.8583, p-value = 6.966e-12
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
cat(decision(runs$p.value, h0="aleatoriedad (Runs test)"), "\n")
Rechazo aleatoriedad (Runs test) (p < 0.05 )

El runs test depende del orden de la serie; con datos ordenados o con estructura temporal suele rechazar aleatoriedad.

Conclusiones

  • t.test() y var.test() permiten inferencia sobre media/varianza con hipótesis bilateral o unilateral mediante alternative.

  • El p-valor guía la decisión al nivel de significación elegido.

  • Para ANOVA: comprobar homogeneidad (Levene) y, si procede, comparaciones múltiples (Tukey).

  • Para justificar inferencia clásica: comprobar supuestos como normalidad y aleatoriedad.
